A well done game, where pretty much the entire design, mechanics works towards you (as a player) feeling in control of a Orwellian surveilence system.

Just beat the game and i must say its a very nice story driven little "Game". Calling it a game is a bit wrong since this is mostly "just" a Choose your own adventure type game, with few elements that actually require thinking. I enjoyed it and played through it in one sitting. Its a bit sad that they dont have any voiceactors that would have given this game considerably more depth. As it stands i didnt regret my decision to buy it. The Story revolves around you working basically for the ingame NSA, except that ingame the NSA has considerably less resources at its desposal. You are tasked in investigating a Terrorist Bombing. You do that by going with a finely toothed comb through the lives of the people who may be of interest. You learn they likes, their dislikes. They sexual Orientation, Their Friends and foes, Their Medical history and so much more. This game manages to show how much of a total strangers life can be found just by the things they say publically. Thought provoking game indeed. Sadly its not much of a game, but i dont regret spending money on it. Btw i beat the game in one sitting, so its not overly long but as i said i dont regret it, but its a YMMV type situation.

A good premise, well caried out. The story grabs you as you are immediatedly made part of it, your choice do matter, even when you think they don't. This gives the possibility of different endings depending on your own values and ideas.

Good game. A lot of reading but compelling storyline. They need to add more as the replay value is jut making the situation turn out different. Random variables and the ability to collect info on all subjects not just the one in question would be nice. If you have a profile on someone and you come across info on an associated person you should be able to capture it. Open up the data chunks! Discovery is limited by the story, so it leaves you just looking for the next Ping notification on what’s relevant. Let the players actually investigate instead of following the investigation that’s laid out. I know you choose what to upload and what not to upload but rounding out the ability to collect data on someone’s info that is staring you in the face is just aggravating. Interesting concept though and the story is good but for what it has in story it lacks in immersion due to not being able to prep data chunks ahead of time until the game lets you.
Phenomenal, thought provoking, piece of art. Absolutely love this game. I cannot wait until season two.

This game is the perfect twisting game that Orwell himself may have imagined were he alive today!

You play an agent of the government keeping the peace throughout the country, seeking out hints that terror attacks may happen, or that people might commit violent crimes. Scrolling through texts, websites and social media pages you build an image of the person you are watching, and start to imagine what crimes they may commit.

Dependant on what information you submit to Orwell, the game will give you different responses and potentially save lives. Either use discretion and submit the minimum information required, or be the true public servant and submit everything, although some information may be useless for them, other information may hold the secret they are after.
i loved it and i want more

Orwell is an intriguing game that does not let you get away with bad jokes. The player will have to use rationality and puzzle together the real story from reading other people's perspectives on the same events, and one must be careful what information is handed over to Big Brother.

The game lets you choose whether you want to let people get away with things or if you hand every piece of information to your superior, and it's easy to let yourself be brainwashed and forget that one surveills real people and not just stains in the system, which the game is really good at making you believe. In addition to this, the game had good sound effects which kept you on the edge of your seat, as well as having many plot-twists and unexpected elements to it. 
Not to mention the witty references to the novel 1984 by George Orwell, which effectively added an element of familiarity to those who are acquainted with the novel.

I recommend this game to both people who know 1984 and to those who don't (and possibly want to), as this is a good introduction to the novel and it gives you an interesting perspective in how it feels to work for Big Brother. Therefore, I give this game a rating of 10/10.

A fun, compelling journey with a very obvious message that starts right from the title.

The story is an exploration through social media and computers.  As a result, it is almost entirely text based, but with musical queues that trigger when a very special/dangerous/important piece of text is discovered.  Great atmosphere, and it does a good job of drawing one in.

Worth a couple of plays to see how minor things pan out, plus the different way it could end. Graphics, characters, concept, all very enjoyable. I've suggested it already to friends to play! Can't wait to see what else this group comes up with.

If you like to read, there's a chance you'll like [i]Orwell[/i], even though it's flawed. If you're wanting an advanced narrative with many branching subplots, however, this probably won't be your cup of tea. 

Still, I like [i]Orwell[/i] overall and recommend it. I'm looking forward to season two. There's potential here. I'm just not sure Osmotic have reached it yet. 

In the case of this "season," the story is too small—not in terms of length, but in terms of complexity. There seem to be at least two possible endings, but, no matter the ending you get, [i]Orwell[/i] mostly forces you to be a particular kind of security agent. It does this by requiring you log certain content on suspects to move forward—even, sometimes, if you don't want to log that content. This was mildly annoying, but I also recognize that greater narrative control usually leads to smoother narratives.

So, what really bothered me was Osmotic botched their message. When playing, you're conscious the developers want you to see the dangers of mass surveillance, but the story ironically shows you its possible value. 

By carefully tracking suspects in the game, you don't just follow tragedies; you can prevent them, or at least make sure they only befall guilty parties. This is because you can't really track anyone who isn't believed to be a few degrees separated from a suspected criminal group. There's very little in the way of stereotyping or racial profiling, though a "supervisor" in the game will jump to conclusions on occasion. 

If this was how mass surveillance worked, people wouldn't be nearly as concerned about it. Pretty sure that's not the message Osmotic was going for.

Overrall I give this a 9/10. And remember, stay vigilant.

When Orwell came out I was very intrigued by it, but from the screenshots, I wasn’t sure how it would be a game, recently my brother had recommended it to me as he knows my love for in depth and hard hitting story games. And I was not disappointed with this, it was in depth and definitely hard hitting where it counted and the only aspect of the game that I knew about when going into it, was the collection of information on people.

First things first, and quite briefly because there isn’t much to say about the graphics of the game. It is based on a user interface that you interact with, whilst it does emulate the use of an actual browser and its contents, it is very clean and takes the realistic nature away from it with its low poly style photos. This was a nice feature as I could focus more on what the story was offering than what the characters looked like and if the modeling of said characters worked with the rest of the interface. The only time there was animation was in the first cut scene where you were introduced to the game, however, this could be either 2D or 3D with flat colours and a low poly style to keep in with the theme. The only thing I was somewhat disappointed with was the fact that there was very little camera work, the game revolves around being monitored everywhere and it is constantly referenced to that cameras are a big thing, yet we do not experience this even though it was shown that they were capable of doing this. It did not, however, subtract from the story that there weren’t any cameras, it just would have been a pretty cool feature.

The graphics made it easy to navigate around the game, making the mechanics for the game very simple as you just had to click and drag certain pieces of information into a data bank, it was simple and easy to get to grips with, it just meant reading and doing a lot of problem solving. That, however, was the allure of the game, filling in the pieces and finding out just what was going on. Due to the dragging of information, you could affect the outcome of the game depending on what pieces of information you decided to let through, this was the coolest feature, I love multiple endings.

8/10 - Very Good

Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.
[*]Music: 1 main repetitive theme loop + some other drama stings...
[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

I purchased this, I think, during last year's Christmas sale and it got sidelined to my backlog of games, but recently played through it.  Afterwards, I regret not having played this earlier as it was an incredible experience and has great writing that kept me off guard throughout the game and made me feel responsible for a lot of what was going on in the game.   

At one point in time, while focusing on the reading and tagging data as I went, I accidentally uploaded a tidbit of a joke from two friends where one was joking that she was being tortured by her friend to get her to go somewhere, and this, without the joking context, was added to a person's bio to incriminate them as a violent and dangerous person.   This, as well as other situations in the game - that were intended rather than my mistake - really drove the point home that the developers were trying to make about the ethics, or lack thereof, of a Big Brother police state.

I'd describe this as a very niche game, if you're into point and click, this is perfect for you. The entire game is presented to you through the Orwell system, where you look into people's data and collect things on them. The game rarely leaves you at a point where you don't know what to do, as important information is highlighted for you, whether this is insane hand holding or reasonable is up to you, I think it's a good thing to have some guidance as to do next.

The story revolves around a government called simply "The Nation" controlled by "The Party(real creative, devs.)" creating a system known as "ORWELL" after a bombing. Along with that, The Party had recently passed something known as "The Freedom Bill" which gives police the right to arrest, interrogate, and detain simply on suspicion of a crime. Basically, The Nation is an authortarian government, it is obviously not as authortarian as Oceania is in 1984, as there is still plenty of resistance to the government, but it is pretty powerful. 

You play as an investigator recently hired by The Nation, living outside of it's borders, tasked to collect information on individuals suspected of the bombing to bring them to justice. Throughout the game, there are several points where you can either choose to be defiant of ORWELL and enter embellished or false information into the system, or choose the blunt option. There are five episodes, and they are all very gripping, the game can actually be reletively creepy at some points as well.

There are multiple endings, as well, which is cool. I won't spoil anything though.

This was a very interesting game. I enjoyed it, story wise, and gameplay wise. Although there were a couple times it crashed on me, I'll blame that on my shit computer, instead of the game. The almost self directed nature of the gameplay, as well as the unique way you could interpret the lives and words of the characters made it very playable, and even re-playable. There were some surprising moments where the internal conflict created was rather intense, and this made for some great moral decisions that would later impact everything, if you made the right or wrong choice. 

Overall, I would certainly recommend the game, as it was very well organized, in depth, and able to capture the attention from any style of player, rule-breaker, rule-follower, and everyone in between.

Orwell is basically a visual novel style game with very limited interactions. At the same time it is quite different from the usual visual novels à la "click this arrow to continue the text".

To me, this game is a refreshing entry in this genre and it did a pretty good job of keeping me interested for the whole time (about 4 hours). I was really immersed into the story and wanted to know what it is all about and what would happen next.

If you are into political thrillers with a focus on government surveillance, conspiracy theories and a hint of mystery then you should consider giving this game a chance.

Edit: After I finished the game I looked up the possible achievements you can get. Without spoiling anything I can say that choices DO matter on several outcomes.

It's currently 4 am at the time of writing. Until I exited the game and saw the clock in the bottom right corner of my computer screen, I was not aware of the time, despite the fact that I'm wearing a watch. That is how enthralling this game is. If you don't want to spend the $10 as of yet (even though it's damn well worth it) get the demo and see if you like it.

Be aware of your choices.

Orwell depicts a utopian setting where individual privacy is constantly violated thanks to public cyber-surveillance in form of an eponymous system, and justified through an ambiguous "Safety Bill" that sanctions "investigative methods" in order to "protect the freedom of The Nation's citizens."
Just how the knowledge about the individual characters' degree of criminal implication does retroactively affect your choices at the different decisive moments of the game makes the second playthrough the more interesting one: if at first you might have been well-intentioned enough to help the surveillance masterminds spying on your fellow citizens, you might be more inclined to rather try sabotaging the system on second thought, at the risk of course, to become yourself a "target" at the end.
That the game makes you second-guessing your "datachunk" choices is its biggest achievement, but that your superiors leave it entirely to you to distinguish between important and irrelevant information is Orwell's patent weakness since too ingenuous fiction-wise, though you need to contribute pertinent data in order to make the story progress, what can also be taxing at times. 
It might not exactly be a totalitarian setting but it still is shocking to realize that the monitoring of both telephone and Internet communications is something also the citizens of democratic countries are faced with, and the game does a good job in showing the use of this type of top-down espionage. Worse still, it is yourself who is doing that closed-circuit observation with Orwell as your user interface: only once a person becomes a “target” related data can be extracted from the different documents and uploaded to Orwell's servers. 
Orwell's approach might be simplified but it likely is how tracking persons in the Cyber Era does work, even when using a variety of sites, personas, and devices. This way the very conflict between public security issues and private data protection is well laid out, albeit far less preoccupying than in the famous Orwellian dystopia. 
The five different episodes can be replayed separately for the different endings, though repeatedly going through the same dialogues quickly loses its interest during replay. Given the subject's topical interest there might be stuff enough for a sequel, unless your investigations did lead to Orwell being canceled altogether...

This is an excellent game, but it is not for everyone. It involves a lot of reading and decision making. There is a great story, but there are also times when you get stuck looking for a clue. The game as a whole gives you an interesting perspective into the world of mass survelance.

In this game, you are the government employee spying on civilians. You read their private posts, listen to their private calls, collect and disseminate information about them, until you have a full picture. It is invasive, horrifying, but might also save lives.
Although, at what cost?

George Orwell and Aldous Huxley would be proud; not in what our society has become, but in what this game truly illustrates what we have learnt from their novels. This is not a university lecture, but a fun game... but at the same time also a game that makes you reflect.
Instead of simply reading about the dangers of how information is used, you get to experience it first-hand, and make your own decisions. Do it well and you prevents horrible things from happening.

But would you be comfortable with powerful - possibly corrupt - governments doing this? Is it worth the danger of being abused?

To say much more is to spoil it, but thankfully (unlike other modern games) there is demo available which allows you to play through the first day of events...so get to it.

Innovative storytelling, a compelling story overall even if i think there is too many "IN YOUR FACE" moment, maybe due to the episodic structure of the game, but they developed some intrestings characters and ethicals dilemnas of utopians groups are well portrayed.

I hope we'll see more game like this, it's definitly a Visual Novel but more engaging.

10/10 must play

An Orwellian story for a modern generation, Orwell offers a look into a world where privacy is moot in the name of the Greater Good. Between the excellent sound design, the responses from the 'voice-in-your-head' handler, and the (not to give too much away) intense and nerve-wracking story, Orwell has provided me a narrative experience perhaps on-par with Spec Ops: The Line. With next to no replay value, the 4-5 hours you'll spend on your first playthrough may be all you put into the game, it is short but still well worth the asking price of £7
An exciting story. The game really makes you think about what you share on the internet.

Orwell provided an engrossing, engaging, and frankly terrifying vision for the future of surveillance and personal privacy. I strongly recommend purchasing and playing the game yourself for this striking experience.

Great game with nice visuals nd the ability to make your own choices which cause different outcomes. I love anything with a rich story and a need to look at all the details, I felt the last chapter/day wasnt quite as good as the others but on the whole it was an enjoyable way to spend a day. Took me about 6 hours to play through in total.

This review is spoiler-free.

I picked up Orwell because I love games that put you in the role of a detective. I previously played "Her Story" and hoped this would be along similar lines (albeit with a different interface), going through data and gaining clues in order to pinpoint suspects.

After playing the game, I was left fairly satisfied and definitely had an enjoyable experience with it, though I did find it lacking in some areas.

The good:
I loved the unique art style, and the whole set up of how you feel like you're logging on to this system as a detective. The music is great and very suitable for the game too, changing in tone dramatically when something in the game changes. I love the overall Orwell theme and how it makes you think about things like government surveillance and whether it's a good or a bad thing. The characters were fairly interesting to me (though mostly unlikable, but that may have been the idea). I enjoyed the way the game is structured and how gathering certain bits of data about a person unlocks more data such as relevant URLs or documents.  I found it intriguing and I wanted to keep on playing after each chapter (there are five chapters in total).

The bad:
The game is pretty short, lasting about five hours, however I do feel like the price point is good for the experience you get. 
I felt like the mechanics of investigation had some excellent ideas but that they could have gone further with it. The game always highlighted where new information was available, and although I suppose that did stop you sifting through all the old documents you had, I kinda wanted to have to do that sifting - as a detective might. It felt a bit too hand-holding as to showing you where to look next, and sometimes that just made it feel like I was just following a path of "look at the new informatiion", "drag it to the person's profile", "look at the new bit of information"... and so on. I think maybe if it wasn't always so obvious which information to go back to, it would have been more fun to find it yourself.

I think in general, I just wanted more of the game, it was definitely a good start, but I would love to see more chapters, or a new story. And maybe an option to not have the right bits of data or documents highlighted, so you had to figure some more stuff out yourself. I think then I would have felt like a more clever detective! 

But all in all, I enjoyed the way the story wrapped up, and a lot of the ideas and mechanics, such as deciding between conflicting information, deciding what to submit and what to ignore to determine what light you put somebody in.. and I enjoyed the end of the game too. 

I think it's a 7/10 for me, an all-round good experience, but lacking in some areas that could have made it more fun/satisfying.

I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

Orwell is one of the most interesting games I've played in a while; it's well thought out, the game experience is smooth and natural and the core elements are solid. It's arguably not a game for everyone but it's a fantastic achievement, that should be beyond doubt.

So who is it for? I guess that's the core question for an indie, niche production such as this so let's get right to it: Orwell is for the player looking for a contemplative, narrative-driven challenge that you can play on your own time. If you like unravelling a mystery carefully, if you like narrative driven games or if you really like surveying people, then this is definitely for you. Who's it not for? It's not for players looking for explosions, fast-paced action or who don't like to read. You read in this game, quite a lot. It's not like reading a novel but expect reading.

In Orwell, you take on the role of an analyst who's trying to unravel a terrorist plot using the governments newest super-surveillance tool, Orwell. The system highlights 'datachunks' in POIs internet activity, chat activity, phone activity, anything really, and it's your job to decide what information is pertinent and what isn't. You build files on suspects while you slowly expand the network of POIs and what you choose to include is what decides the 'system's' attitude towards groups and individuals. Of course, the question soon beckons; should you be doing any of this?

As the story moves forward, the player is confronted with many choices and they have real consequences for the story, not merely symbolic ones. Furthermore, while the system highlights important information, some decisions can only be made accurately through the players own memory and deductions from text pieces that at the time perhaps seemed inconsequential. It's a game that rewards the player for keeping up and thinking for themselves.

Review:

Orwell is a love letter to Orwellian fiction. It is a plot filled with mystery and intrigue that evolves fast enough so you will never think about getting bored. I especially enjoyed how the game doesn’t paint the organization you work for as inherently bad/evil. Flawed, but in a way that makes it real, not malicious. This gives each individual person the chance to come to their own conclusions about this potential future.

There are a few issues with this game such as certain data chunks having potentially vague outcomes (much like a Bioware dialog wheel). Also the slow writing in personal messages, while realistic, did get a bit tiresome where you can read the text 3 times faster than they can type. And sadly you cannot walk away, wait for the convo to finish, and then come back, as certain data chunks are time sensitive (I learned this lesson the hard way). All those issues are trivial however and I did not feel that they ever interfere with my ability to play and enjoy the game; a minor annoyance. The ending however, did rub me the wrong way. 

Without spoiling anything, I will just say that the ending is multiple choice depending on how you act. Initially I enjoyed this reveal, yet ended up accidentally choosing an ending I did not want, after not being bale to figure out how to select the one that would make the most sense with my character/play style. Then once I realized what I had done I tried to go back, however once you beat the game that save file is forever stuck at the epilogue after the choice. This requires you to complete an additional play through.

With all that said I would definitively recommend this game!

Summary: A pretty good game that makes you think about how people see things from different perspectives. From the Government's point of view: you're doing a good thing. From the citizen's point of view: invasive and controlling. As you play this game you will constantly think about this as you go through your work. As far as I'm aware, there are 3 endings to the game, and make for roughly 3-5 hours playthrough depending on how quickly you work through it.

Positives: 
-A game that makes you think. If you're like me and you try and solve the game before it's over, it will have you guessing yourself over and over, because the ending is not quite who you suspect. (Even if you do guess correctly - it's not likely through the means that you're thinking.)
-The style of the game is very pretty and modern, with the futuristic features being clean and eye catching. Personally, I loved the layout and setting of the game.
- Time IS important! Like in real life, if you find critical information that might affect something in your life and don't immediately act to stop it, you may face consequences. (I learned the hard way when I Alt + Tabbed out of the game for a minute.)

Negatives:
-Not many, honestly. The story was great and consistent and always had you going back to double-check your infirmation. (Great thing imo, but I guess people can see this as tedious.)
- There are occassionally blips where it says there is more possible information for you to look at, but there isn't.
- It's too short in my opinion. You only really play 'one' story, and I feel like you should be able to play a couple more than that, and the ending you get should influence it too.
